source: Lei, Yan, Momo, Cohen (2026) Learning Reusable Agent Subroutines from Experience (ARISE)
finding: Closest hit for gap 1. Steps from correct ReAct traces get a short move-name label from an LLM, labels are merged into 5-10 categories, ranked by frequency, and the top K become LLM-executed subroutines. This is automatic subgoal discovery from text reasoning traces.
numbers: Five tasks (MuSR murder/object/team, RuleArena NBA, NatPlan meeting). Five-task mean: DeepSeek-V3 67.4 vs ReAct 38.8 and best baseline ACE 56.6; Gemini 2.5 Flash 77.7 vs ReAct 68.2, CoT 69.3, AWM 71.6 (+6.1), ASI +11.5. AIME 2023-24 (43 problems): 79.1 vs ReAct 44.2, AWM 58.1 (Flash-Lite); 81.4 vs CoT 79.1 (Flash).
quote: Whether induced knowledge helps at all depends on its execution interface.
limits: No token-matched comparison against hand-written or prompted decomposition. Baselines are other learned memories (AWM, ACE, ASI), not a human-written subgoal list. Trip planning: only 2 successful traces, near-zero accuracy for all methods. Single run per cell, small test sets. Frequency ranking, not bottleneck detection.
agent_relevance: Frequency-ranked move categories from solved traces are a cheap, working way to seed a subgoal library. The matched-token control against a hand list is still missing, so keep it as a test.

source: Lei et al. (2026) ARISE, interface and content ablations (Table 2, Section 5.2, Appendix F)
finding: The same induced text helps only when it is run as a separate sub-call. Read as in-context skill text it can hurt. Removing the induced content while keeping the interface also hurts.
numbers: Gemini 2.5 Flash mean: skill-document delivery 66.1 and code-tool delivery 69.8, vs subroutine delivery 77.7 and ReAct 68.2. DeepSeek-V3: skill 51.8, code 48.3, subroutine 67.4. Generic instruction in place of induced specs: 78.4 to 67.7; generic names too: 64.2. Cost per task: ACE $13.14 vs ARISE $3.63 on Gemini; DeepSeek ARISE $5.23 (NBA alone $21.26).
limits: Interface and content effects measured on 5 tasks and two models; cost not matched to a decomposition baseline.
agent_relevance: A subgoal is worth most as an isolated sub-call with its own context, not as advice text. Supports O-decompose as separate calls.

source: Lei et al. (2026) ARISE, library size K (Table 9, Appendix G)
finding: Direct LLM measurement for gap 3. A small library of 3 to 5 induced subroutines is enough. K=10 was never best.
numbers: DeepSeek-V3, K=3 / 5 / 10: murder 80.0 / 75.0 / 77.0; object 71.7 / 68.9 / 51.9; team 61.0 / 68.0 / 62.0; NatPlan meeting 49.0 / 51.0 / 45.0. K=3 and K=5 differ by at most 7.0 points per task. Libraries had five subroutines on most tasks, four on NBA, one on meeting. Min support m=3 per category.
quote: The K=10 library is never best in this sweep.
limits: Single evaluation per cell, no confidence intervals; object task drops 17 points at K=10 but others by 1 to 6. Only three sizes. Library limited by how many categories reach support 3.
agent_relevance: Sweet spot for language subgoals looks like 3 to 5, in line with kSubS k=3-4 and the four eigenoptions. Cap the active subgoal set near 5.

source: Lei et al. (2026) ARISE, trace filtering and tool sensitivity (Table 3, Table 10)
finding: Learning from correct traces only helps when the full spec is hidden from the agent prompt. Libraries from generic text-search tools matched those from expert-designed tools.
numbers: Generic vs hand-designed collection tools: murder 86.0 vs 87.0, object 75.5 vs 70.8. MuSR DeepSeek-V3 variants A (correct, hidden) 75.0/68.9/68.0; B (correct, visible) 69.0/68.9/63.0; C (any, hidden) 74.0/66.0/60.0; D (any, visible) 70.0/67.0/73.0.
limits: Differences of a few points on small test sets; mixed across tasks (variant D best on team).
agent_relevance: Verification (correct-only filter) is useful but not dramatic at induction time. Keep the subgoal spec out of the main prompt and in the sub-call.

source: Prasad et al. (2023/2024) ADaPT: As-Needed Decomposition and Planning with Language Models (re-read for gap 2)
finding: Re-opened to check the cost control. ADaPT matched LLM CALLS, not tokens, against Try-Again and Reflexion. There is no always-decompose ablation: Plan-and-Execute is a fixed one-shot plan, not recursive decomposition at every node. GPT-4 was tested only as ADaPT vs its own executor.
numbers: GPT-3.5: ADaPT beats ReAct by 28.3 pts (ALFWorld), Plan-and-Execute by 28.3 and Try-Again by 23.8 (ALFWorld), Reflexion by 14.1 overall. WebShop: up to 27 over ReAct, Reflexion +9, LATS +6. TextCraft: +33 over ReAct, +25 over Plan-and-Execute, +20 over Reflexion. TextCraft recipe depth 2: ReAct 26.9 to ADaPT(dmax=4) 78.2; depth 3: 1.8 to 38.7; mean max depth used 1.9 and 2.8. GPT-4 gain up to 37 pts on TextCraft, LLaMA-2-70B up to 15. Weak ALFWorld executor 3.3 to 41.7.
limits: Calls, not tokens, are matched, and the paper says baselines often use fewer calls. 2023 models only. Relies on the executor's own success judgment (the paper's Limitations cite Huang et al. and Stechly et al. on self-verification).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open for frontier models. Decompose-on-failure is cheap in calls but its edge on frontier models and at equal tokens is unmeasured.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Select-Then-Decompose, EMNLP 2025 Main (Oral)
finding: Explicit decomposition buys little on simple reasoning but costs 4 to 10 times the tokens. Execution model size matters more than decomposition model size. A selector that picks the approach per task sits on the performance-cost Pareto frontier.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, GSM8K: CoT 93.17% at 396 tokens; Plan-and-Solve 92.72% at 468; ReAct 91.66% at 2700 (6.81 calls); Plan-and-Execute 92.34% at 2443 (5.13 calls); P&E(DAG) 90.67% at 1943; Select-Then-Decompose 93.56% at 517 (1.28 calls). Trivia Creative Writing: P&E uses 10x the tokens of the highest implicit approach; P&E(DAG) about 4x implicit. Qwen2.5 1.5B/7B/14B: scaling the executor gives larger gains than scaling the decomposer; distilled R1 models produce more invalid plans at 14B.
limits: Not ADaPT: ADaPT is listed only as related work, not run as the central arm. Mostly GPT-4o-mini and Qwen2.5 sizes; math, writing, coding, not agent tasks.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that always-decompose loses at equal tokens on easy items, and that a router (decompose only when the task needs it) wins. Supports an as-needed rule for O-decompose.

source: Liu, Chen, Zhang (2026) Lost in Implicit Routing: How LLM Agents Fail to Load Relevant Skills at Scale
finding: Gap 3 and 5 from the other side: library size hurts retrieval. With the right skills installed and irrelevant skills added, agents stop loading skills.
numbers: SkillsBench tasks, golden skills fixed. 0 to 1,000 irrelevant skills: loaded-skill recall 73.6% to 27.4%; zero-load rate 9.3% to 51.6%; Pass@3 51.6% to 38.6%. Explicit selection from the same library keeps 73.9% recall. Libraries up to 10,000 skills tested. Masking only descriptions of irrelevant skills largely restores loading.
limits: Irrelevant skills here are distractors from other tasks; a real subgoal library has near-duplicates, which may be worse. Executable verifier per task.
agent_relevance: A subgoal library must be pre-filtered (small active set), not left for the agent to scan. Another reason for a cap near 5 active subgoals.

source: Zhou, Rong, Lin, Zhang (2026) Many Steps into One: Reasoning Contraction and the Limits of Safe Memory Reuse for LLM Agents
finding: First direct LLM measurement for gap 5. Stored reasoning macros go stale when facts change. Success/failure vote counters (ExpeL/ACE style) are slow change detectors. A likelihood-ratio detector plus a certificate that restarts when facts change removes most stale answers.
numbers: KQA-STREAM, Qwen3-8B, 30 streams of 200k queries. Live reasoning acc. 0.379; fold-once memory with no retirement 0.534 acc with 1,290 stale answers per 10^4 queries; ExpeL-style counter 967 stale, ACE-style 946; SPRT+LR-CUSUM 54; recommended rule 0 stale (perfect edit notices), 16 with own detector only; accuracy 0.648 with 21% fewer LLM calls. Across five LLMs counters serve 7.0 to 13.5 times more stale answers than certified memories; on 521 EvalPlus code tasks with an exact test 35 to 73 times more. Counters leave about half of 156 stale memories in service at stream end vs 2% for the likelihood-ratio rule. LR detector alone cuts stale answers 9 to 12 times vs invalidation alone.
limits: Facts-and-templates memory, not subgoal libraries as such; edits are synthetic KB edits plus a Wikidata timeline. With mild natural staleness, counters were 3.5 points more accurate than the strict rule (folding pays when staleness is small). Authors' own preprint, not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: Answers which rule works: an explicit edit/version notice plus a test run or verifier beats counting votes. A subgoal stored with a re-checkable test should be retired by that test, not by a success tally.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) Trackable Skill Library Lifecycle Management for Agentic RL (TrackRL)
finding: Skills in a library follow different paths: redundant once internalized, still useful as scaffolding, or harmful. Co-retrieved skills free-ride on each other so ordinary credit counts mislead. Per-skill randomized injection inside each GRPO group gives skill-level evidence.
numbers: ALFWorld seen/unseen with GPT-5.6-Luna reflector: TrackRL 78.1/71.9 vs SkillRL 62.1/58.2. Gemini-2.5-Flash: 68.8/70.3 vs D2Skill 66.4/69.5. Skill-free mode: TrackRL (Luna) 72.7/64.1 vs D2Skill 61.7/58.6 and GRPO 58.6/53.0. Harmful skills are removed and blocked from re-admission.
limits: RL-trained policies, not prompt-only agents. Margins vs D2Skill under Gemini are under 3 points. The count of harmful skills and the size of the harm were not captured in the lines read.
agent_relevance: Gives the mechanism for gaps 5 and 8: measure each stored subgoal against a skill-free control episode before keeping it.

source: Xia et al. (2026) SkillRL: Evolving Agents via Recursive Skill-Augmented Reinforcement Learning
finding: A two-level library (general plus task-specific skills) beats a flat one, and distilled skills beat raw trajectories. Library grows from 55 to 100 skills during RL.
numbers: ALFWorld 89.9% success, WebShop 72.7% (GRPO base 77.6 on ALFWorld, +12.3). Ablations: no hierarchy (task-specific only) -13.1 pts ALFWorld, -11.3 pts WebShop; raw trajectories instead of skills up to -25 pts; no cold-start SFT about -20; no dynamic evolution -5.5. Library: 12 general + 43 task-specific at start, 20 + 80 at step 150.
limits: RL-trained model with a strong teacher for distillation; no control with the same diverse samples but no structure, so gap 8 is not closed. Authors list retrieval noise as the library grows as an open issue.
agent_relevance: Structure (general vs specific levels) carried 11 to 13 points over a flat skill list. Weak evidence that structure, not just more samples, matters; the same-sample flat control is still missing.

source: Hao & Li (2026) Automating SKILL.md Generation for Computer-Using Agents via Interaction Trajectory Mining
finding: Counter-evidence. Mining skills by segmenting and clustering GUI trajectories gives readable clusters but no reliable downstream gain and loses to a trivial frequency baseline.
numbers: 5 of 8 clusters have purity of at least 0.95 vs InteraSkill Workflows labels. GRPO on Qwen3-8B: IW skill-step accuracy 18.5% to 20.5%; WebArena 55.8% to 44.2%; BrowseComp+ 43.5% to 43.3%. Auto-generated SKILL.md beats a hand-written table at N=100, 250, 2000 but not N=500, 1000; Frequency baseline better at every size (normalized edit distance 0.485 vs 0.528 at N=2000).
quote: A cluster can be coherent without being useful.
limits: Weak 8B policy, GUI actions, boundary detector cuts at large action changes (not bottlenecks). Authors call it a diagnostic study.
agent_relevance: Readable clusters are not enough. Compare any discovered subgoal library with a frequency prior before trusting it.

source: Peng et al. (2023) Self-driven Grounding: LLM Agents with Automatical Language-aligned Skill Learning (SDG)
finding: Earlier form of subgoal clustering: LLM-proposed subgoal descriptions are embedded, clustered with k-means (k chosen by Calinski-Harabasz score), and one RL skill is trained per cluster. Authors note unsupervised clustering adds some noise.
numbers: Ablations on restoring the initial state and on the deduction step are shown as curves; no single headline number was captured in the lines read.
limits: Only the method and ablation text was checked; no matched-token comparison with hand-written subgoals. RL grid environments (BabyAI-style), not text reasoning.
agent_relevance: Shows the clustering step is not new in 2026; the open question is a matched control, not the idea itself.

source: Shek & Tokekar (2025) Option Discovery Using LLM-guided Semantic Hierarchical RL (LDSC)
finding: An LLM proposes the subgoal sequence and skill chaining builds options per subgoal. Reported to beat DSC, DDPG and Option-Critic on grid and robot maps.
numbers: Authors report average +55.9% over baselines, 53.1% shorter completion time, +72.7% success on their maps (abstract and introduction; the per-map table was not re-derived).
limits: Simulated navigation with hand-built key-door maps; relative percentages; no eigenoption or covering-option arm, so gap 7 is not tested.
agent_relevance: LLM-supplied semantic subgoals can replace graph-based option discovery in small worlds. Does not settle bottleneck vs covering.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) Evaluating Cognitive Maps and Planning in LLMs with CogEval (re-read for gap 6)
finding: Re-checked the community-graph result. LLMs hallucinate edges, take long paths and loop on community graphs, and failures rise with sparsity within blocks. BFS or DFS instructions helped only some settings. Only GPT-4 was used in the density sweep; no reasoning model or external graph tool was tested.
numbers: GPT-4, 30 runs per setting. Shortest path to a state 1 cluster away: success 0 of 30 at temperature 0; not above 10% at temperature 0.5 or 1. BFS/DFS prompts helped cluster counting on graph D at temperature 0 and 0.5 but less at 1; for one-cluster-away paths only BFS at temperature 0.5 improved. Block density swept from line graph to clique with five vertices per block.
quote: out of 30 runs GPT-4 has a success rate of 0 at temperature 0
limits: 2023 models, text edge lists, no bottleneck-first choice test, so human effects like Solway's 4.4x are not directly replicated.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. Do not assume the agent sees community structure in a text graph; give it an explicit graph tool or compute it.

source: Lu et al. (2025) AgentRewardBench: Evaluating Automatic Evaluations of Web Agent Trajectories
finding: LLM judges of whether a whole trajectory succeeded are not reliable. No judge exceeded 70% precision, so about 30% of accepted trajectories were failures. No judge led on every benchmark. Rule-based checks missed many true successes.
numbers: 1,302 expert-reviewed trajectories, 5 benchmarks, 4 agent LLMs, 12 judges. Best precision under 70%. Rule-based recall 55.9%. Screenshot-only input gave higher precision than screenshot plus accessibility tree.
limits: Judges whole-task success, not subgoal reached or still valid. Web agents only.
agent_relevance: A self-judged subgoal reached is likely wrong in the false-accept direction about 30% of the time. Use an executable check where possible and treat LLM judging as a screen.

source: Pignatelli et al. (2024) Assessing the Zero-Shot Capabilities of LLMs for Action Evaluation in RL (CALM)
finding: CALM has an LLM split a task into subgoals and judge whether each is achieved in a transition. Re-opened to confirm the tables report F1, accuracy, precision, recall and TP/TN/FP/FN against human labels, and that F1 varies with LLM size.
numbers: Human-annotated MiniHack demonstrations; per-model rows in Tables 1-4 and a size sweep in Figure 1. The 0.16 F1 figure in earlier claims was not re-derived row by row here.
limits: Preliminary, zero-shot, no verifier arm. Authors tie errors to NetHack knowledge gaps.
agent_relevance: Consistent with d15: judging subgoal state with a bare LLM is weak. The gap-4 verifier arm is still unmeasured.

source: Search-result report: Talk, Evaluate, Diagnose (2026) and MobileJudgeBench (2026)
finding: Search snippets only. A 2026 user-aware agent evaluation defines progress as the share of subgoals a judge marks achieved, with repeated runs and majority vote. MobileJudgeBench (931 human-annotated trajectories, 6 judge methods, 5 backends) reports that elaborate judge pipelines do not reliably improve quality and the backbone model dominates.
limits: Not opened; not subgoal-level accuracy. A pointer only.
agent_relevance: Suggests majority vote over repeats and a stronger backbone beat clever judge prompts. Unverified.

source: Search coverage note for gaps 7, 9 and 10 (no new primary paper found)
finding: Within the search budget of this run, no 2023-2026 study was found that compares covering, eigen and bottleneck options on a learned or noisy graph; measures a problem-size threshold at which hierarchy pays for LLM reasoning; or replicates the pseudo-reward prediction error with larger samples. arXiv search pages began returning HTTP 429 and WebSearch hit its shared quota.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search, not proof. These gaps need a later search pass.
agent_relevance: Treat gaps 7, 9 and 10 as open design uncertainty.
